Efficiency options

Author

Marie-Hélène Burle

Training runs into two walls: not enough memory and not enough time. This course has already covered several solutions; this page goes over the remaining ones and ends with an efficiency options summary.

Packages

import copy

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

Gradient accumulation

We promised this one when discussing batch sizes: when the batch you want does not fit in memory, simulate it with several smaller microbatches whose gradients add up. Since backward() accumulates into .grad by default, the mechanism is almost free:

class Tiny(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(32, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

torch.manual_seed(42)
batch = torch.randn(64, 32)
labels = torch.randint(0, 10, (64,))
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

The claim to verify: four microbatches of 16, each contributing loss / 4, produce the same gradients as one straight batch of 64. Same starting weights, so a copy of the model for each path:

reference = Tiny()
accumulated = copy.deepcopy(reference)  # same starting weights as reference

loss = loss_fn(reference(batch), labels)
loss.backward()
ref_grads = [p.grad.clone() for p in reference.parameters()]

reference.zero_grad()  # not needed anymore, but a clean habit
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(accumulated.parameters(), lr=1.0)
optimizer.zero_grad()
for micro_x, micro_y in zip(batch.split(16), labels.split(16)):
    loss = loss_fn(accumulated(micro_x), micro_y) / 4  # loss / N
    loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

acc_grads = [p.grad for p in accumulated.parameters()]
print([torch.allclose(a, b, atol=1e-5) for a, b in zip(ref_grads, acc_grads)])
[True, True, True, True]

The gradients match (up to floating-point noise, hence the tolerance): mathematically, one batch of 64 and four accumulated microbatches of 16 are the same update. In a training loop, the pattern is:

for i, (x, y) in enumerate(train_loader, start=1):
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y) / ACCUMULATE
    loss.backward()
    if i % ACCUMULATE == 0:          # one optimizer step per group
        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        scheduler.step()
  • zero_grad moves to the end of the group; the scheduler steps once per effective batch.
  • The caveat: layers with cross-sample state, above all batch normalization, see only one microbatch at a time, so their statistics are computed over 16 rather than 64 images. Our CNN has none; our fine-tuned ResNet-18 does. Usually acceptable, occasionally the reason results shift — know which kind of layer you are accumulating through.
  • Accumulation trades time for the illusion of a large batch: it does not speed anything up. When the goal is throughput rather than memory, a real large batch on more hardware is the honest lever.

Mixed precision, recalled

bf16 autocast is the default of this course wherever the GPU has the units for it; it halves activation memory on top of speeding up compute. Two precisions we have not used:

  • fp16, the older half-precision, needs gradient scaling (GradScaler) to avoid underflow. Reach for it only on pre-Ampere GPUs where bf16 is emulated — a vanishing category.
  • 8-bit and 4-bit: quantization (the torchao library) shrinks trained models for inference, and 8-bit optimizer states (bitsandbytes) cut optimizer memory at training time. Both are drop-in-ish, both trade a little accuracy; measure rather than assume.

Activation checkpointing

The other memory eater after parameters and optimizer state is activations: every intermediate result the forward pass produces, kept alive until backward() needs it. Memory grows with depth, resolution, and batch size.

Activation checkpointing (recomputation) throws most of them away and recomputes them on demand during the backward pass:

def forward(self, x):
    for block in self.blocks:
        x = checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False)  # recompute in backward
    return self.head(x)

One call per block; the block’s inputs are kept, its internals are not, and the backward pass runs the block again to rebuild them. Expect roughly a third more compute for a large drop in activation memory. It composes with everything else in this course — FSDP2 and torch.compile both support it — and it is the standard companion to sharding when even a sharded model’s activations overflow.

Asynchronous checkpointing

Large-model checkpoints take minutes to write, and the naive torch.save freezes the training loop while it serializes gigabytes. Two patterns to know:

  • Write to the compute node’s local disk ($SLURM_TMPDIR) and copy back asynchronously, rather than writing straight to the network filesystem.
  • For sharded models, DCP’s asynchronous save serializes on a background thread.

Summary

Symptom First lever Then
GPU idle between steps (low utilization) DataLoader workers, prefetch, pinning cheaper transforms
Steps themselves slow torch.compile TF32 / bf16
Batch does not fit in memory gradient accumulation (this page) smaller batch + lr adjustment
Model state does not fit on one GPU FSDP2 8-bit optimizers
Activations do not fit activation checkpointing (this page) smaller microbatch
Epochs too slow overall more GPUs, DDP profile first: where does the time go?

Two habits hold the menu together: profile before optimizing, and change one thing at a time — every lever above interacts with the learning rate.

Your turn:

Add an --accumulate N option to train.py (batch 64/N per microbatch), run two epochs on the full data with N=4, and compare the epoch losses with a normal two-epoch run.

  • Hint: the loss is divided by N inside the loop; optimizer.step(), zero_grad(), and scheduler.step() fire every N microbatches.
  • Hint: our CNN has no batch normalization, so the comparison is clean.
